title: Harbor Town weather report
provenance: Prewritten, source-reviewed demo; no live AI request.

story.overview: This is the starting file for a small weather-report program. When run directly, it sends Harbor Town and three readings (18, 22 and 20) to make_report, then prints the returned message.

chapters.title: Gather readings and display the report
chapters.beginner: Create the sample readings, request a report for Harbor Town, and print it.
chapters.developer: Create the sample readings, request a report for Harbor Town, and print it. The readings are fixed example data; no weather service is contacted.
chapters.storyBeginner:
Pip is waiting in the front room when his friend main opens a job card. Three temperature slips are laid on the workbench: 18, 22, and 20. main puts them together in a list and gives the bundle the local name readings. That name lets the next instruction refer to the whole bundle. A second package holds the town name, Harbor Town.

The job card names coworker make_report as the friend who can turn those supplies into a message. main does not do the averaging here. It also does not choose warm or mild. Those jobs belong to helpers in other rooms. Pip carries the town name and the reading bundle together on one request. At the other workbench, the town name will be called city, while the bundle will still be called readings.

When make_report sends back a text reply, main can hand that reply straight to print. The code does not store the message under a new local variable first. Printing puts a message on the noticeboard; it is different from returning that text to another caller. main has no explicit return statement of its own. Its useful visible effect is the display request. We will open make_report’s job card next, then return here to see how that reply is used.

story.overview: make_report turns a city label and temperature readings into one formatted message. It asks average in units.py for the mean, labels temperatures of at least 25 as warm and all others as mild, and returns the message.

chapters.title: Connect to the averaging helper
chapters.beginner: Make average from units.py available to this file. Its body runs only when invoked.
chapters.developer: Make average from units.py available to this file. Its body runs only when invoked.

chapters.title: Build the weather message
chapters.beginner: Average the readings, choose warm or mild at the 25-degree boundary, and return a message formatted to one decimal place.
chapters.developer: Average the readings, choose warm or mild at the 25-degree boundary, and return a message formatted to one decimal place. Expects readings that support averaging and a city value usable in a formatted string.
chapters.storyBeginner:
Pip steps into the report room with the town package and the reading bundle. Friend make_report knows them by the local labels city and readings. The helper needs a single temperature for the message, so it asks coworker average for help. That friend works in units.py. Pip takes the readings along, while make_report keeps the city label ready for the final message.

At average’s workbench, the same incoming bundle gets the local name values. A new name inside a helper does not by itself mean a new bundle was copied. When average finishes, its numeric reply comes back to make_report. Here, that reply is given the label temperature. This is the handoff that connects the calculation in one file to the decision in another.

Now make_report faces its dilemma: is temperature at least 25? If yes, the helper writes warm on a label. Otherwise, it writes mild. The helper does not need to take both paths. It then combines city, temperature, and the chosen label into a single text message. The temperature is written with one digit after the decimal point, and C appears as text beside it. Pip can carry the completed message back to main. This helper returns the message; main is the coworker that asks print to show it.

story.overview: average returns the arithmetic mean of a nonempty collection by dividing its sum by its length. For an empty collection, it returns 0 instead.

chapters.title: Find the mean of the readings
chapters.beginner: Return 0 for empty input; otherwise return sum(values) / len(values).
chapters.developer: Return 0 for empty input; otherwise return sum(values) / len(values). Returning 0 for empty readings is a rule in this code, not a measured temperature. Nonempty items must support numeric averaging.
chapters.storyBeginner:
Pip reaches the calculation room and meets friend average. The bundle handed to this workbench is called values here. The local label is different from readings in the report room, but this request still carries the caller’s supplied readings. The helper’s first instruction is a check for an empty bundle.

If there are no readings to use, the job card says to reply with 0. That path ends the job before the division. The zero is a choice written by the programmer; it is not a temperature measured from an empty bundle. With a nonempty bundle, the other instructions can continue. sum adds the values, and len counts how many items there are.

Dividing that sum by that count makes the mean. For the supplied slips, 18 plus 22 plus 20 is 60. There are three slips, so the static calculation predicts 20. Nothing in this body writes into the supplied list. It calculates a reply from it and returns that reply to its caller. Pip can now carry the number back to make_report, where the number receives the label temperature. From there, it can help decide which weather label belongs in the message.

projectStory.title: A weather report finds its way home.
projectStory.opening:
Pip arrives at the workshop with a town name and three temperature slips. The town is Harbor Town. The slips read 18, 22, and 20. Someone wants those pieces turned into one easy-to-read weather message.

No one helper does every part. main gathers the supplies, make_report prepares the message, and average works out the number in the middle. We will follow their request through the rooms, then follow the reply back home.
projectStory.ending:
The reply can now travel back through the report room to main. In this example, the three readings add up to 60, and there are three readings. Their mean is 20. Because 20 is below 25, make_report chooses mild rather than warm.

The message comes back as “Harbor Town: 20.0 C, mild”. main can put it on the noticeboard with print. The outer __name__ check allows this starting visit only when main.py runs directly.

That outcome is a static prediction from the included inputs and instructions. CodeStory has not run the file or called a model to produce this demo.
